question: What structural modifications in small molecules and polymers improve electrochemical performance of conjugated carbonyl compounds in rechargeable batteries?
answer: Structural modifications that improve the electrochemical performance of conjugated carbonyl compounds in rechargeable batteries include enhancing conjugation to stabilize redox-active carbonyl groups, designing rigid molecular frameworks to mitigate dissolution, and incorporating electron-withdrawing groups to increase redox potentials. Polymerization of small molecules into extended networks improves electronic conductivity and reduces solubility in electrolytes. Composite formation with conductive additives (e.g., carbon) addresses poor intrinsic conductivity, while tailored electrolyte systems (e.g., weakly coordinating solvents) minimize dissolution. For sodium/potassium-ion batteries, flexible molecular structures accommodate large ion radii, and hybrid designs combining n-type carbonyls with p-type materials enable all-organic cells. Future optimization requires precise control of molecular packing (tap density), electrode composition (<40% carbon), and mechanistic studies to link structure-property relationships.

The paper aims to review the potential of organic carbonyl compounds as cathode materials for lithium, sodium, and potassium ion batteries, emphasizing their advantages such as high theoretical capacity, low cost, and structural diversity. It provides an overview of recent research on small molecules and polymer-based carbonyl materials and discusses strategies to address challenges like dissolution in electrolytes, low discharge voltage, and poor electronic conductivity.
